{{Short description|British mathematician, artist and author}}

'''Edmund Orme Harriss''' (born 1976 in [[Worcester, UK]]) is a British mathematician,<ref name=imperial>[https://www.imperial.ac.uk/events/97715/experiencing-mathematics-edmund-harriss/ Experiencing Mathematics – Edmund Harriss at Imperial College London] 11 December 2018</ref> writer<ref name=flood/> and artist.<ref>[http://gallery.bridgesmathart.org/exhibitions/2019-joint-mathematics-meetings/edmundharriss Mathematical Art Galleries:  Edmund Harriss] [[Bridges Conference]]</ref> Since 2010 he has been at the Fulbright College of Arts & Sciences at The [[University of Arkansas]] in [[Fayetteville, Arkansas]] where he is an Assistant Professor of Arts & Sciences (ARSC) and Mathematical Sciences (MASC). He does research in the Geometry of [[Tessellation|Tilings and Patterns]],<ref name=imera/> a branch of [[Convex geometry|Convex]] and [[discrete geometry|Discrete]] Geometry.<ref name=gate>[https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Edmund-Harriss Edmund Orme Harriss] at ResearchGate
</ref> He is the discoverer of the spiral that bears his name.<ref name=guardian>[https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2015/jan/13/golden-ratio-beautiful-new-curve-harriss-spiral The golden ratio has spawned a beautiful new curve: the Harriss spiral] The Guardian, 13 January 2015</ref>

==Education and career==
Harriss earned a [[Master of Mathematics]] at the [[University of Warwick]] (2000) and then obtained his PhD at [[Imperial College London]] (2003) with the dissertation "On Canonical Substitution Tilings" under Jeroen Lamb.<ref>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref>

Harriss has been a speaker at [[FSCONS]], a Nordic Free software conference.<ref>[https://wiki.fscons.org/FSCONS_2009/Summary FSCONS 2009/Summary] FSCONS wiki</ref>

Harriss is active on [[Numberphile]] where he has given talks on [[Heesch number]]s, [[Tribonacci number]]s, the [[Rauzy fractal]] and the [[plastic ratio]].<ref>[https://www.numberphile.com/videos/category/Edmund+Harriss Edmund Harriss videos]</ref>

In May and June 2020 Harriss was a visiting fellow at The Institute for Advanced Study of [[Aix-Marseille University]] (IMéRA) where he studied the possibilities of visual and spatial models and animations to illustrate a wide variety of mathematical ideas.<ref>[https://imera.univ-amu.fr/en/resident/edmund-harriss-1 Edmund Harriss: Visiting Fellow] IMéRA - Institute for Advanced Study</ref>

==Mathematical art==
[[File:MetalCurvahedraBall.jpg|thumb|350px|Sculpture made from flat materials using the curvahedra invented by Harris<ref name=gazette>[https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2019/aug/31/mathematician-s-ua-art-multiplies-20190-1/?fbclid=IwAR3au7Ki8f7IrjEOHqYBiugLdPhzaVRLq2ckJzQU96Lvlg5S7p%20Ul7LcFNc Mathematician's UA art multiplies], [[Arkansas Democrat-Gazette]], August 31, 2019</ref>]]
The [[Gauss–Bonnet theorem]] gives the relationship between the curvature of a surface and the amount of turning as you traverse the surface’s boundary.<ref>[https://2020.bridgesmathart.org/regular/137.html Gauss-Bonnet Sculpting], by Edmund Harriss, Bridges 2020</ref> Harriss used this theorem to invent shapes called Curvahedra which were then incorporated into sculpture.<ref name=curvahedra>{{cite journal |last1=Harriss|first1=Edmund |date=2020 |title=Gauss-Bonnet Sculpting |url=http://archive.bridgesmathart.org/2020/bridges2020-137.html |journal=Proceedings of Bridges 2020: Mathematics, Art, Music, Architecture, Education, Culture |volume=2020 |pages=137–144 |isbn=978-1938664366}}</ref> Scientists at MIT are investigating ways in which curvahedra may have applications in construction.<ref name=mit/>

Art and mathematics are intertwined in Harris's work.<ref name=imera>[https://imera.univ-amu.fr/en/system/files/cv_harriss_edmund.pdf Edmund Harriss bio] Aix-Marseille University</ref> He uses public art to demonstrate deep mathematical ideas<ref name=mit>[https://news.uark.edu/articles/58031/honors-college-gearharts-dedicate-curvahedra-sculpture Honors College, Gearharts Dedicate Curvahedra Sculpture] University of Arkansas NEWS, Oct. 21, 2021</ref> and his academic work frequently involves the visualization of mathematics.<ref>[https://www.arkansasonline.com/news/2019/aug/31/mathematician-s-ua-art-multiplies-20190-1/ Mathematician's UA art multiplies; Large outdoor campus work in plans] by Jaime Adame, [[Arkansas Democrat-Gazette]], 31 August 2019</ref>  Mathematically themed sculptures by Harriss have been installed at [[Oklahoma State University–Stillwater|Oklahoma State University]],<ref>[https://casinfo.okstate.edu/spotlights/1364-mathematics-learning-success-center-to-unveil-artwork Mathematics Learning Success Center to Unveil Artwork] OSU College of Arts and Sciences</ref> at the University of Arkansas,<ref name=courtyard>[https://aplus.uark.edu/courtyard-curvahedra/ Courtyard Curvahedra], By Kendall Curlee, University of Arkansas: A+ Online 2021</ref><ref>''[https://news.uark.edu/articles/59280/experience-the-beauty-of-mathematics-in-courtyard-curvahedra- Experience the Beauty of Mathematics in 'Courtyard Curvahedra']'' University of Arkansas Newa, March 09, 2022</ref> and at [[Imperial College London]].<ref name=imera/>

Combining his interest in art and mathematical tilings he is one of 24 mathematicians and artists who make up the [[Mathemalchemy]] Team.<ref>[https://mathemalchemy.org/team-24-mathematicians-artists-of-mathemalchemy/ Mathemalchemy’s Team]</ref><ref name=duke>[https://today.duke.edu/2021/11/art-installation-celebrates-beauty-and-whimsy-math Art Installation Celebrates the Beauty and Whimsy of Math] Duke Today, November 9, 2021</ref>
{{clear}}

==Harriss Spiral==
[[File:Golden and Harriss Spiral Story 4.pdf|thumb|350px|The Harriss Spiral]]
Harriss noticed that the [[golden ratio]] is just one example of a more general idea: In how many ways can a rectangle be divided into squares and rectangles?  The golden ratio results when a rectangle is divided into a one square and one similar rectangle.  But by varying the number of squares and sub-rectangles, we arrive at what Harriss calls "proportion systems".  The solutions in all cases are algebraic numbers and the golden ratio is just one of them.<ref>[https://gigazine.net/news/20150115-harriss-spiral/ "Spirals of Harris" thought inspired by the beauty that the golden ratio produces] Gigazine.net (in Japanese), Jan 15, 2015</ref>

: "The golden ratio is this incredibly well-explored corner of a whole city,” he said. “I wanted to give signposts to other locations in that city."<ref name=guardian/>

Harriss investigated the next simplest case, dividing a rectangle into one square and ''two'' similar rectangles.  The ratio that emerged in this case is the so-called [[plastic ratio]].<ref name=chalk>[https://chalkdustmagazine.com/regulars/on-the-cover/on-the-cover-harriss-spiral/ On the cover: Harriss spiral] by Matthew Scroggs and Edmund Harriss, Chalkdust Magazine, 14 March 2019</ref> The [[golden spiral]] is closely related to the first case, dissection into one square and one similar rectangle.  Harriss applied the same idea to this second case and discovered a new [[fractal]] [[spiral]] related to the [[plastic ratio]] and since named after him.<ref name=guardian/>
{{clear}}

==Selected publications==
===Books===
Harriss has published several books designed to spread joy in mathematics.<ref>[https://theexperimentpublishing.com/creator/edmund-harriss/ Edmund Harriss]  The Experiment Publishing</ref> The sales of his colouring books run well beyond 100,000.<ref name=flood>"[https://www.theguardian.com/books/2015/jul/06/colouring-in-books-boom-continues-with-volume-of-mathematical-patterns Colouring-in books boom continues with volume of mathematical patterns]", by Alison Flood, [[The Guardian]], 06 Jul 2015</ref><ref>"[https://www.wired.com/2015/11/math-coloring-book/ You're Never Too Old to Color—Especially Math Patterns]", by Angela Watercutter, [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] Nov 30, 2015</ref>

* (2015) ''Snowflake Seashell Star: Colouring Adventures in Numberland '' with Alex Bellos {{ISBN|1782117881}}<ref>"[https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/coloring-by-numbers-mathematically/ Coloring By Numbers, Mathematically]", by Chau Tu, [[Science Friday]], February 1, 2016</ref>
* (2016) ''Patterns of the Universe: A Coloring Adventure in Math and Beauty'', with Alex Bellos {{ISBN|9781615193233}}<ref>"[https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aad9853 Patterns of the Universe A Coloring Adventure in Math and Beauty]", [[Science Magazine]], 01 Jan 2016, Vol 351, Issue 6268, p. 36</ref>
* (2016) ''Visions of the Universe: A Coloring Journey Through Math's Great Mysteries'', with Alex Bellos {{ISBN|9781615193677}}
* (2020) ''Hello Numbers! What Can You Do? 'An Adventure Beyond Counting'', with Houston Hughes, Illustrated by Brian Rea {{ISBN|9781615196845}}

===Papers===
* (2011) [https://www.nature.com/articles/475166a "From oranges to modems" in "The unplanned impact of mathematics"], Nature, vol 475, pp. 166–169
* (2011) "[https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/2011-363-09/S0002-9947-2011-05188-3/ Algebraic numbers, free group automorphisms and substitutions on the plane]" with Pierre Arnoux, Maki Furukado and Shunji Ito, [[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] 363 (2011), pp. 4651-4699
* (2015) "[https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1500633112 Strain and the optoelectronic properties of nonplanar phosphorene monolayers]" with Mehrshad Mehboudi et al, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
* (2020) "[https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10586458.2022.2102094 Algebraic Number Starscapes]" with [[Katherine E. Stange]] and Steve Trettel
